question: Can a simple surrogate learn how arbitrary subsets of internal model components affect a prediction, and can that surrogate guide targeted zero-shot model edits?

key_findings.claim: COAR reframes component attribution as supervised prediction over intervention masks rather than assigning importance from a single gradient or one-at-a-time ablation.
key_findings.evidence: For each example, the method samples fixed-size random component subsets, actually ablates them, records a scalar model output, and fits a linear regression from the binary keep-mask to that output. Coefficients therefore summarize average effects under the chosen multicomponent ablation distribution; they are not context-free intrinsic meanings of neurons or filters.

key_findings.claim: The learned linear surrogates predict held-out random ablations substantially better than standard component-importance baselines.
key_findings.evidence: Across CIFAR-10 ResNet-18, ImageNet ResNet-50, and ImageNet ViT-B/16, COAR has the highest per-example Pearson correlation. At 5% ablation for ImageNet ResNet-50, mean correlation is 0.65 versus 0.34 for leave-one-out; on CIFAR-10, correlation falls from 0.74 at the trained 10% ablation rate to 0.68 at 15%. Correlation measures rank/linear association, however, not absolute calibration or counterfactual error.

key_findings.claim: COAR-EDIT finds small ablation sets that produce strong targeted behavior changes across five vision editing tasks.
key_findings.evidence: Reported edits include correcting ImageNet errors with median aggregate accuracy loss at most 0.2%; reducing one class from 66% to 20% by ablating 8/22,720 filters; raising Waterbirds worst-group accuracy 64% to 83% and CelebA 47% to 85%; restoring triggered CIFAR-10 accuracy 37% to 84%; and raising CLIP typographic-attack accuracy from 51% to 89% synthetic and 54% to 86% real. The component count k is selected per task, often by validation performance.

key_findings.claim: Selective class degradation is not certified machine unlearning, and editing by zero ablation is intentionally coarse and reversible.
key_findings.evidence: The paper calls one task 'forgetting,' but it only suppresses accuracy through filter ablation; it does not remove training-example influence, test reconstruction/privacy leakage, compare retraining, or certify deletion. The authors explicitly state that ablation is not component removal and that COAR-EDIT is not intended as a state-of-the-art editing method.

key_findings.claim: The method's scalability claim is relative to combinatorial search, but its intervention dataset is extremely expensive.
key_findings.evidence: Main vision setups use 50,000, 100,000, and 200,000 ablation samples; GPT-2 uses 200,000 counterfactuals for each of 1,000 evaluated sequences and Phi-2 uses 100,000 for 500 examples. Each sample is described as a model forward pass, followed by a high-dimensional regression. Experiments use machines with nine A100/V100 GPUs; 2-5x sample reduction causes only a small quality loss but does not remove the basic cost.

key_findings.claim: Language-model evidence supports counterfactual prediction but not language-model editing or mechanistic circuit discovery.
key_findings.evidence: For GPT-2 TinyStories, mean correlations are 0.83-0.89 across 1-5% held-out ablations; for Phi-2 BoolQ they are 0.58-0.66. These appendices do not perform edits, assess generated behavior, test larger instruction models, or recover a known circuit. Nearly all claimed editing utility comes from vision classifiers.

key_findings.claim: Linearity works locally in mask-distribution space but degrades under distribution shift, exposing unmodeled component interactions.
key_findings.evidence: Prediction correlation declines when test ablation fractions differ from training and when larger subsets more strongly damage the base model. The authors propose nonlinear component models as future work. Scaling activations rather than zeroing them yields related attributions, yet all interpretations remain intervention-specific and off-distribution activation shifts are not eliminated.

method.core_idea: Learn an example-specific surrogate of the model's response to component masks, then invert that surrogate to choose a targeted intervention.
method.mechanism: Collect real ablation counterfactuals, regress scalar output on binary component keep indicators, compare target/reference coefficient distributions with t-statistics, and ablate components with the most favorable differential scores.
assumptions: Random fixed-fraction ablations span the intervention neighborhood relevant to downstream edits.
A linear additive surrogate adequately compresses interactions among ablated components.
Zeroing or scaling selected weights/activations defines a meaningful causal intervention despite activation distribution shift.
A scalar margin captures the behavior one wants to understand or edit.
Small target/reference samples and validation-selected k generalize to the intended deployment distribution.

techniques.role: Fits an additive prediction surrogate from sampled counterfactual interventions.
Produces a separate coefficient vector for each evaluated example.
Ranks components by a two-sample coefficient statistic for selective editing.
Changes behavior without gradients or parameter retraining by disabling selected components.

evaluations.setting: ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 and ResNet-50/ViT-B16 ImageNet component masks
evaluations.metric: Per-example Pearson correlation on unseen ablations
evaluations.result: COAR consistently leads baselines; ImageNet ResNet-50 at 5% is 0.65 versus 0.34 leave-one-out
evaluations.baseline: Leave-one-out, gradient-times-parameters, neuron conductance, and internal influence

evaluations.metric: Correlation between predicted and actual component counterfactuals
evaluations.result: GPT-2 0.83-0.89; Phi-2 0.58-0.66 depending on ablation fraction

evaluations.setting: ImageNet per-example correction and class suppression
evaluations.metric: Target margin/accuracy and aggregate collateral accuracy
evaluations.result: Small filter sets fix errors with median collateral loss at most 0.2% and reduce a target class 66% to 20%

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 backdoor and CLIP typographic attacks
evaluations.result: 37% to 84% for backdoor; 51% to 89% synthetic and 54% to 86% real typography

limitations: Author-stated: counterfactual collection requires very many forward passes.
Author-stated: results depend on an ablation method that can shift activations off distribution.
Author-stated: COAR-EDIT is coarse ablation, not a competitive general editing algorithm.
Author-stated: linear models lose predictive power for out-of-distribution ablation fractions.
Reviewer-identified: Pearson correlation does not establish calibrated counterfactual magnitudes or faithful mechanistic decomposition.
Reviewer-identified: editing experiments are overwhelmingly vision-only and select edit size using task-specific validation feedback.
Reviewer-identified: no uncertainty, multiple-testing correction, or stability analysis is attached to the component t-ranking.
failure_modes: Strong component interactions make additive coefficients inaccurate for targeted combinations.
Zero ablation creates behavior caused by distribution shift rather than removing the component's ordinary computation.
A surrogate trained at one mask fraction extrapolates poorly to a much smaller or larger edit.
Reference examples miss a collateral subgroup, so an apparently selective edit harms unmeasured behavior.
Class suppression is mistaken for data deletion or knowledge erasure.
Counterfactual collection becomes infeasible for frontier-scale models and fine component granularity.
reusable_insights: Interpretability can be evaluated as held-out intervention prediction rather than qualitative plausibility.
Attributions are conditional on a component granularity, intervention operator, output statistic, and mask distribution; all four should be recorded.
Editing is a strong downstream faithfulness test, but must include broad collateral evaluations and comparison to task-specific editors.
Surrogate calibration and interaction residuals should accompany correlation when counterfactual estimates drive action.
open_questions: Can structured or active mask sampling reduce forward passes by orders of magnitude?
Do sparse quadratic or low-rank interaction models materially improve out-of-fraction extrapolation?
Can COAR guide weight updates rather than reversible ablations while retaining specificity?
How stable are selected components across seeds, equivalent parameterizations, and activation-repair interventions?
Does component modeling scale to instruction-tuned generative models and sequence-level behaviors?
Can formal unlearning metrics distinguish behavior suppression from information removal?

competitive_landscape.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
competitive_landscape.difference: ROME localizes factual recall through activation interventions and applies a rank-one weight update; COAR predicts arbitrary multicomponent ablations with a regression surrogate and mainly edits vision models by zeroing components.

competitive_landscape.title: Does Localization Inform Editing? Surprising Differences in Causality-Based Localization vs. Knowledge Editing in Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Shows causal-tracing localization often fails to identify the best edit layer; COAR instead evaluates its attributions through actual targeted edits, but only offers limited LM editing evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Attribution Patching Outperforms Automated Circuit Discovery
competitive_landscape.difference: Uses two forward passes and one backward pass to linearly approximate activation-patching effects on circuit edges; COAR uses many real forward interventions to fit a more empirically accurate mask surrogate.

competitive_landscape.title: DisCEdit: Model Editing by Identifying Discriminative Components
competitive_landscape.difference: Directly identifies components discriminating edit targets for model editing; COAR first learns reusable example-level counterfactual models and then derives differential edit scores.

competitive_landscape.title: Modifying Memories in Transformer Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Updates Transformer weights with constraints designed to preserve unrelated outputs; COAR-EDIT requires no training but is limited to disabling components and has weaker generative-model evidence.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Component modeling operationalizes understanding as counterfactual prediction, and COAR provides scalable, useful component attributions that directly enable editing.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Held-out ablation prediction across architectures/modalities and five quantitatively strong editing case studies support the operational framework and regression approach.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Treating component interpretation as supervised mask-response modeling is a clear, testable synthesis of perturbation and surrogate ideas. Its practical scope is constrained by enormous intervention cost, linear/intervention-specific semantics, and coarse mostly-vision editing; it should not be read as mechanistic explanation or certified forgetting.

reviewer_notes: Read all 61 pages, including language-model appendices, sample-size and ablation-method studies, editing details, and limitations (page 61 is blank in the source extraction). Competitors were checked against primary NeurIPS, arXiv, and OpenReview records on 2026-08-23.
